book: 207 - Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique
samples: Held's introduction frames Wonder Woman as an ambiguous figure - a sexy superhero, feminist icon, even a god - and borrows Simone de Beauvoir's term 'ambiguity' from The Second Sex to name women's bind: acquiesce to gender norms and lose yourself, or become yourself and lose your place. He runs through Diana's either/ors (Steve Trevor, Themyscira or Boston, mortal or god, American or cosmopolitan) and argues she creates an identity only by defining herself against each expectation. Because everyone is torn between what they are and what they want to become, he concludes we should embrace Wonder Woman's contradictions and stake our commitments while living in ambiguity.

Wright reads Wonder Woman's 75-year history through Beauvoir's 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman,' arguing Diana's move from Paradise Island to Man's World - surrendering eternal life for Steve Trevor - enacts the hard-won transcendence of immanence that The Second Sex demands. She shows the comics alternating between empowerment (Marston's 'woman of tomorrow,' an unpatriotic George Washington scolding women war workers) and regression (Trevor persuading Wonder Woman to marry and type memos about women's place being the home, the 1990s hyper-sexualized art), evidence that woman remains the Other to man's Subject. Wonder Woman's durability, she says, lies in exactly this ambiguity, and like Beauvoir's woman of tomorrow she models forging identity through projects in the world.

Donovan uses the New 52 Azzarello run's gods as a catalogue of gender stereotypes - jealous Hera hunting Zola, woman-incinerating Apollo, hyper-masculine First Born, self-sacrificing Demeter - then tracks Hera's transformation after Apollo makes her mortal as a Beauvoirian passage from immanence (being Zeus's Other, defined by his desire) to transcendence (charting an independent identity, aiding baby Zeke). Foucault's Panopticon explains how gender norms are internalized without an enforcer, and Butler's drag example grounds the claim that Wonder Woman accepting the god of war mantle - leading a female Amazon army 'not as your princess but as the god of war' - is a subversive performance of gender.

A mother-daughter pair tracks Wonder Woman's and Harley Quinn's costume histories (the 1990s Artemis-era near-thong Diana, the New 52 brothel-styled Harley) and argues with Aristotle that sexualized drawing strips both characters of phronesis, the practical wisdom a virtuous agent needs - the wisdom by which an outmatched Wonder Woman talks Strife into carrying her to safety and Harley exploits the Joker's vanity to beat him. The paradox: the more provocatively each is drawn, the less she can succeed as moral hero or anti-hero, since objectification replaces goal-directed cunning with one-dimensional sex display. The New 52's armor-clad, Hephaestus-consulting Wonder Woman shows phronesis restored.

McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (systematic, moral, altruistic, radically atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) using Wesley Autrey's Harlem subway save against Captain Sullenberger's Hudson landing, and argues Wonder Woman is genuinely heroic because her mission is voluntary and supererogatory - she wins the contest to leave Paradise Island and can retire to it at will, unlike a compulsory Superman. He then uses the demoted, powerless Diana Prince era with I Ching to show her deeds stay in principle replicable, like Batman's rather than Superman's. The payoff: Wonder Woman works only as a 'super hero' who inspires imitation, which is how 'we' answer the problem of evil - why innocent people suffer destructive, ruthless evil.

Zanin surveys 75 years of Wonder Woman - Marston's bondage-inflected feminism (the Ordeal of a Thousand Links, bracelets that forfeit power to any man who chains them), Kanigher's romance-era drift, the 1968 Diana Prince fashion-bouticless era that opened just as feminists protested Miss America, and the Taco Whiz years - to ask whether 'wonder woman' has become an unattainable ideal that belittles women. Reading through Beauvoir's analyses of woman as Other, imposed femininity as immanence, and the body as situation, she argues the superwoman 'have it all' standard is a feminist faux pas, yet closes with Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity: rather than resent her perfection, women should accept the challenge on their own terms instead of acquiescing in mediocrity.

book: 208 - X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse
samples: After the acknowledgments and an introduction, this block runs two essays. Hopkins's 'The Lure of the Normal' uses Storm, Rogue, Beast, and the Morlocks plus the mutant 'cure' to dissect descriptive vs. prescriptive 'normality,' citing Foucault on the monster/individual-to-be-corrected and Nietzsche's Zarathustra to frame transhumanist vs. bioconservative attitudes to enhancement. Southworth's Wolverine essay argues personal identity via Locke's memory theory (the Xavier/Cassandra Nova body-swap) and Parfit's fission (Madrox's duplicates, Wolverine's repeated brain trauma), concluding that many distinct 'persons' have inhabited Wolverine's body.

Four-plus essays. White defends Jean Grey's altruistic suicide in the Dark Phoenix Saga through Kant's categorical imperative (both formulas) and the confl icting-duty case of the rabid-dog letter, ranking deontology over utilitarian and virtue readings. Kavadlo reads the X-Men as existential literature, tying Sartre's bad faith and anti-Semitism and Camus's Sisyphus to the mutants' Jewish/Holocaust roots and never-ending serial struggle. Burnett uses Mister Sinister, Sentinels, and eugenics to trace bioethics through Spencer's evolutionary ethics and Galton. Dunn casts Layla Miller as Bacon's 'knowledge is power' against Aristotle's contemplative ideal. The Davis 'Magneto, Mutation, and Morality' essay begins here, opening the evolutionary-ethics question of Xavier vs. Magneto.

This block finishes Davis's essay (Xavier's 'good nonsense' rules vs. Magneto/Dennett/Hobbes evolutionary morality) then runs several more. Robichaud's 'Professor X Wants You' weighs whether Storm should join the X-Men or Brotherhood using Nozick's experience machine (Rogue vs. 'Eugor') for well-being and Dworkin's civil-disobedience tiers for when violent resistance is permissible. Housel's 'X-Women' reads Jean Grey, Rachel Summers, Scarlet Witch, Storm, Mystique, Rogue, and Kitty through Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' bad faith, Ortega's project, and Baudrillard. McWilliams uses Singer's speciesism and human-rights declarations to ask if mutants deserve moral consideration and whether torture/experimentation on them can be justified. Darowski reads Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks as postmodern metafiction raising Plato's-cave ontological questions.

book: 209 - Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint
essays: Building Communities One Gym at a Time
To Hack or Not to Hack
The Zen Master and the Big Aristotle
Playing for the Same Team Again
Plato and Aristotle on the Role of Soul in Taking the Rock to the Hole
samples: The editors' introduction surveys how basketball is woven into American pop culture (Jordan, Shaq, films like Hoosiers and White Men Can't Jump, March Madness) and previews the volume's questions: how to measure greatness, whether intentional fouling is unethical, whether Zen improves a jump shot. It frames fans' MVP arguments (citing Ric Bucher's joke acronyms) as implicitly philosophical in their demand for defined terms, and notes Naismith was himself a philosophy major, making hoops 'the thinking person's game.' It applies no single philosophical doctrine, serving instead as a roadmap to the essays that follow.

Webb uses Indiana high school basketball to argue the communitarian case against liberal individualism: drawing on MacIntyre, Sandel, and Walzer, he contends communities (not rights-bearing individuals) are the source of meaning, and that small-town gyms like the New Castle Fieldhouse were public spaces that built genuine community. He reads Rick Mount's choice of hometown fame over the pros, the Milan miracle, and the abolition of Indiana's single-class tournament as evidence that mass media and national sport replace real 'face-to-face' communities with 'virtual' ones, using Conseco Fieldhouse's nostalgic theming as his prime example of that loss.

Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.

Kretchmar defends a 'modified purist' view that team-oriented, fundamentals-based basketball is generally better than the individualist modernist game, offering three arguments. The functionalist argument borrows Searle's account of constitutive rules to say ten-person interactive complexity makes a richer, more durable 'test' (like chess vs. tic-tac-toe); the variety argument uses Mill's On Liberty to warn that market pressures homogenize basketball toward football; and the communitarian argument uses MacIntyre's notion of a 'practice' with internal goods to show ESPN Streetball's isolated one-on-one feats erode basketball as a cooperative practice.

Bassham and Hamilton distill six success principles from coaches Smith, Pitino, Summitt, and Krzyzewski and show each echoes great philosophers, treating the court as a 'dojo' or place of enlightenment. Setting goals and pursuing excellence through habit map to Aristotle's eudaimonia and doctrine of habituation (Shaq the 'Big Aristotle' given the Nicomachean Ethics by Phil Jackson); the emphasis on outworking adversity and controlling only one's own effort maps to Stoics like Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius, as when Summitt and Dean Smith tell players to control what they can and accept the rest.

Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.

essays: Vince Lombardi and the Philosophy of Winning
Football and Aristotle'S Philosophy of Friendship
Inside the Helmet What Do Football Players Know
Virtue and Violence Can a Good Football Player Be a Good Person
What's so Bad about Performance-Enhancing Drugs
“They Don't Pay Nobody to Be Humble!” Football's Ego Problem
Crowning a True Champion The Case for a College Football Playoff
Upon Further Review Instant Replay Is an All-or-Nothing Affair
Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League
samples: Belliotti reconstructs Vince Lombardi's 'winning isn't everything, it's the only thing' as a deeper philosophy of pursuing excellence and perfection as process values, not victory as such. He rebuts Marxist charges (via Sage) that competitive sport is mere capitalist superstructure by arguing, with Marx and Nietzsche, that hard creative labor and self-overcoming are human goods in themselves rather than mere capitalist demands. Lombardi is cast as a 'grand transcender' whose danger of fascism arises only when winning becomes an end in itself.

Fry uses fumbles—Tony Romo's botched hold, Jerome Bettis's near-disaster saved by Roethlisberger, Leon Lett's showboating—as psychodramas illustrating the fragility of the good life. He invokes Aristotle's worry that one cannot call a life happy until it is complete, and Thomas Nagel's 'moral luck' (the negligent truck driver) to argue our culpability for fumbling, on the field and in life, is shaped by contingency, so responses should be discriminating. He draws on Frankfurt on caring and closes on redemption through effort, luck, and grace.

Gallagher maps Aristotle's three kinds of philia onto football: friendship of utility (the quarterback needing his offensive linemen), of pleasure (Friday-night high school and college ball), and of shared goodness (Bo Schembechler's bond with Anthony Carter, who deflected reporters to teammates). He reads the Steelers dynasty and Paterno's locker-room 'love' through Aristotle's 'concord' and 'a single soul in two bodies,' and answers Bertrand Russell's worry about violent competition by insisting football is grounded in philia, not enmity.

Geivett uses football to illustrate epistemology, distinguishing factual (propositional) from competence (skill) knowledge through what running backs and quarterbacks must know and enact under split-second pressure, including 'football physics' vectors on a rollout pass. He treats the athlete's need to be mindful of knowledge amid stadium noise as a lesson in reliable belief, then critiques classroom skeptics who deploy Descartes's evil-demon and the brain-in-a-vat thought experiment, arguing mere logical possibility is no evidence for skepticism.

Parker asks what pleases football fans and argues the answer is beauty, framed around a Michael Vick scramble against the Ravens. He applies Kant's Critique of Judgment—beauty as disinterested, an end in itself, and its judgments nonconceptual yet universal ('you should too')—to explain why fans watch games rather than read box scores, and why skilled offensive play by Barry Sanders or Joe Montana strikes us as beautiful. Using Ted Cohen's 'circles of taste' and an informal survey, he concludes beauty admits of degree and depends on the viewer's grasp of context.

Davison defends a 'Violence Principle'—intentionally causing violent harm known to be unnecessary for a greater good is wrong—and applies it to in-the-rules football hits like Jack Tatum on Darryl Stingley and Warren Sapp on Chad Clifton. Against a consequentialist defense of intimidation, he invokes Kant's requirement to treat persons as ends, not mere means, arguing players consent to accidental injury but not intentional harm. Citing the Socratic examination of the soul, he warns of moral danger to players who use excessive force and to fans who relish violence for its own sake.

book: 211 - Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links
essays: First Hole Golf and the Importance of Play
Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf
Third Hole Finding the (Fair)Way with Confucius and Ben Hogan
Fourth Hole “Quiet…Please!” Reflections on Golf and Civility
Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character
Sixth Hole Virtue Ethics From Caddyshack to Better Golf
Seventh Hole Cheating and Gamesmanship among Amateur and Professional Golfers
Eighth Hole Playing Through Racism and Sexism in Golf
Ninth Hole Is Golf Inherently Irrational
Eleventh Hole Philosophy in the Kingdom Golf, Mysticism, and Philosophy
Twelfth Hole Midround and Midlife Defining Moments
Thirteenth Hole Free and Easy Wandering on the Golf Course Swing Like a Taoist
Fourteenth Hole Plato and Confucius on the Form of Golf From the Real to the Ideal
Fifteenth Hole The “Ideal” Swing, the “Ideal” Body Myths of Optimization
Sixteenth Hole Golf and the Meaning of Life
Seventeenth Hole More Than a Playing Partner Golf and Friendship
Eighteenth Hole Swing Thoughts Tough Questions for a Tough Game
samples: Andy Wible's introduction argues that if Plato and Aristotle were alive they would be avid golfers, because both golf and philosophy seduce great minds with problems that look easy yet prove endlessly difficult. It frames golf as 'a Sudoku that cannot be solved' and pairs it with the eternal questions (right and wrong, who am I, beauty, God, meaning) to preview the volume's chapters. Golf becomes a vehicle for the examined life, enlivening philosophy through the lived experience of the game.

Al Gini defends play as intrinsically valuable and essential to being human, drawing on Huizinga's three criteria of 'true play' and William James's ideal of the amateur who plays 'for the love of it.' Using his golf-obsessed father as an extended case, he shows how golf functions as a self-contained, absorbing 'refuge from ordinary life' that delivers completion, coordination, and cooperation, echoing Plato's claim in the Republic and Laws that sport forms both person and community. The chapter treats golf as an end in itself whose joy sustains a flourishing life rather than as a means to external reward.

Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.

Laumakis builds an analogy between pursuing excellence in golf and living a flourishing human life, then contrasts two models. Reading Confucius's Great Learning and Analects onto golf, he casts a repeating swing as a 'well-ordered kingdom' rooted in self-cultivation, and reinterprets ren, li, yi, and xiao so the 'authoritative player' masters the game through ritual practice, a teacher-parent (xiao), and doing what is appropriate in each lie. Against this social conception he sets Ben Hogan's Five Lessons as a 'rugged individualist' account stressing solitary practice and personal responsibility, and proposes a contextual pluralism as a mean between communitarian absolutism and individualist relativism.

McNaron argues that golf promotes civility both empirically and normatively through its rules (self-scoring, self-called penalties) and its etiquette (silence during a swing, care for the course). Using an Aristotelian virtue-ethics frame plus Kekes's 'conduct according to custom' and Calhoun's expressivist account of civility as communicating respect, he treats civility as a mean acquired by habituation and opposes it to skloka, the petty hostility of win-at-all-costs sport. He defends golf's quiet against charges of classism, reads Tiger Woods's outburst at a shutter-clicking photographer as justified anger at an etiquette breach, and names the Ryder Cup's jingoism, boorish spectators, and intrusive media as threats to golf's civil, contemplative character.

Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.

Michael Austin argues that a truly Olympic greatness requires moral, not merely athletic, excellence, reading Aristotle's magnanimity (megalopsychia, 'greatness of soul') as the crowning virtue that unifies all others. He tests this against three Olympians: bobsledder Eugenio Monti, who lent a rival team a part and lost gold; sprinter Wilma Rudolph, who forced her homecoming parade to be integrated; and runner Emil Zatopek, who gave away his gold medal and defied the Soviet invasion of Prague. Using Robert Adams's idea of 'modules of virtue,' he explains why some champions show self-control in sport but not in life, whereas the magnanimous person holds every virtue across every domain.

Raymond Belliotti reads the twenty-year Olympic career of Italian sprinter Pietro Mennea, 'The Southern Arrow,' through Machiavelli's concept of virtu, the excellence relevant to one's function that lets a person master Fortuna. He distinguishes Machiavelli's military, political, civic, moral, and artistic virtu (using the Agathocles passage and the Life of Castruccio Castracani) and argues Mennea's physical prowess, mental toughness, and turning of anti-southern prejudice into motivation exemplify athletic virtu. Machiavelli would scoff at Olympic ideals of peace and brotherhood but relish the fierce international competition and the discipline of sport that Mennea embodied through his 1980 Moscow gold and later political career.

Scott Parker argues that distance runner Steve Prefontaine, who finished a medal-less fourth at Munich 1972, embodied the true essence of the Olympics better than any champion, an essence he identifies with Nietzsche's 'higher man' and Emerson's self-reliance rather than winning. He aligns Pre's front-running, effort, confidence, and will with Nietzschean self-overcoming and life-affirmation and Emersonian self-valuation, arguing value is what the valuer assigns himself through hard work. Reading Pre's exhausted stumble to the finish as a possible enactment of amor fati, love of fate, Parker holds that if Pre did his best he should love rather than merely accept his defeat.

Paul Cantor and Peter Hufnagel use Nietzsche's essay 'Homer's Contest' to argue that the competitive spirit the Greeks called thumos links philosophy and athletics, presenting Plato's dialogues as 'the Olympics of philosophy' in which Socrates is the last man standing. They trace thumos as the spirited third part of the soul in Plato's Republic, the guardians' quality that reason must tame through gymnastics and music, and as the force Socrates enlists to win the thumotic youths Glaucon and Adeimantus to philosophy. They then read Achilles in the Iliad and its funeral games in Book XXIII as a build-up/discharge/calm cycle of thumos, offering athletics as Homer's alternative channel for the same warlike energy.

Through an imagined Greek play featuring the Spartan 'trembler' Aristodemus and an Avery-Brundage-like IOC president, Jesus Ilundain-Agurruza argues for rethinking the Olympic motto and creed around three Greek virtues, aretE (excellence), andreia (courage), and kalon (noble beauty), grounded in Aristotle's virtue ethics, the mean, and eudaimonia. Using the Spartans exercising on the eve of Thermopylae, he defends a collaborative, non-instrumental conception of competition against record-obsession and cheating, exemplified by Eugenio Monti and Cecil Healy. He closes with Camus's Sisyphus, arguing the athlete pushes the rock in the spirit of aretE, spending energy joyfully 'just because,' turning punishment into sport.

Heather Reid interprets the Olympic Charter's first Fundamental Principle through the ancient ideal of aretE, arguing the metaphysical structure of sport, contests that create purposeless obstacles, exists to cultivate and celebrate human excellence rather than to beat opponents or make money. Citing Plato the wrestler, Suits's definition of game-playing, and Homer's funeral games, she maps five virtues onto sport: eusEbeia (reverence for ideals beyond oneself), andreia (courageous endurance in agOn), sOphrosynE (harmonious power and control), dikaiosynE (justice as rule-order and proper function), and sophia (the athlete's pursuit of truth about human capacity, akin to 'flow'). The goal she proposes is the 'Olympian soul.'

book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About
essays: Why Roger Federer Is the Best Or Is It McEnroe
Why Are All Tennis Films Bad
Excuses, Excuses Inside the Mind of a Complainer
Authoritarian Tennis Parents Are Their Children Really Any Worse Off
“You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis
Love–Love A Fresh Start at Finding Value and Virtue in Tennis
Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play
The Ridiculous Meets the Radical in the Battle of the Sexes
samples: Editor David Baggett frames the collection with his own lifelong love of tennis (watching the 1980 Borg-McEnroe Wimbledon final, idolizing Borg and Gerulaitis) and argues tennis is an ideal springboard for philosophy, glossing 'philosophy' as the etymological 'love of wisdom.' He invokes Plato's idea that instances of beauty in this world make the heart ache for beauty's truest source, applying it to the sublime excellence of great play. He positions the whole book as using tennis to reach questions that matter, including the meaning of life, citing David Foster Wallace's quip that the title Tennis and the Meaning of Life is 'redundant.'

David Foster Wallace argues that watching Roger Federer live at Wimbledon delivers a near-religious experience because top sport is a prime venue for 'kinetic beauty'—a beauty rooted in human beings' reconciliation with the fact of having a body. He reads the 2006 Federer-Nadal final as a clash of the Apollonian (Federer's clinical northern artistry) against the Dionysian (Nadal's martial southern machismo), and dwells on specific Federer Moments (the reverse-thrust forehand winner against Agassi at the 2005 US Open) as instances where an athlete seems exempt from physical law. He treats Federer's grace as ineffable, defining it by what it is not, and juxtaposes the transcendent beauty of the body against the suffering body of cancer-survivor coin-tosser William Caines.

David Baggett asks who is the all-time best male tennis player and treats it as a genuine problem in metaphysics ('what is the case?') and epistemology ('how do we know it?'), surveying candidates from Tilden to Federer against ten criteria. He argues the sentence 'Federer is the all-time best' is vague, running the tennis-ball-losing-an-atom sorites through three theories of vagueness—fuzzy logic, supervaluationism, and Timothy Williamson's epistemicism, which he favors: there is a fact of the matter (God knows it) but our closeness-to-the-margin ignorance keeps us from knowing it. He uses Anselm's ontological argument and Guanilo's perfect-island reply to distinguish the all-time best from the best-possible player, and invokes Sartre's existentialist rejection of mere potentiality ('could've/should've') to insist he is asking who actually was best, not who might have been.

Mark Huston argues no truly great tennis film—a 'Raging Bull of tennis'—will ever be made, and builds his case through genre theory. He contrasts an Aristotelian essentialist approach to defining a genre (necessary and sufficient conditions, as in Noel Carroll's Poetics-derived definition of horror) with a Wittgensteinian 'family resemblance' account, adopting the latter to identify overlapping-but-nonessential core features of the sports film (representing a real sport, literal not merely metaphorical emphasis, a culminating sporting moment, an athlete protagonist). Reading Nobody's Perfect, Wimbledon, and Tennis, Anyone...?, and citing David Foster Wallace on how tennis's speed is essentially untelevisable, he concludes tennis's un-representability on screen plus the genre's uplift bar it from the aesthetic seriousness that wins critical greatness.

Kevin Kinghorn, drawing on interviews with coach Brad Gilbert, dissects why tennis players and their parents complain and make excuses. He catalogs cognitive biases and the vividness effect (why a bad call, like McEnroe's 'You cannot be serious!' outburst, sticks and feels like persecution) as forms of irrationality, and notes Stoicism (which he attributes to Zeno) as a philosophy that would suppress the complaining temperament. His central mechanism is Freudian self-deception: citing Freud's hypnotized-umbrella subject who invents a reason for his own behavior, he argues tennis parents pretend their child is destined for greatness and then genuinely come to believe the lie, so excuse-making becomes a self-destructive sign a player will never be a champion. He also reads Andrea Jaeger's ambivalence about winning as evidence of mixed, partly unconscious motivations.

Kevin Kinghorn asks whether authoritarian tennis parents (like the family of prodigy Jan Silva) harm their children's well-being, and tests three theories of the good life. He rejects Aristotle's perfectionist eudaimonia because the 'uniqueness of reason' criterion fails, substituting his own perfectionist-yet-mental-state view that well-being consists in the felt experience of connecting with others. He defends a Mill-style hedonism of higher and lower pleasures against Robert Nozick's experience-machine objection, arguing the machine only refutes the claim that we desire mental states, not that well-being consists in them, and dismisses desire-satisfaction theories and Feinberg's 'right to an open future' as failing to show that lost autonomy itself lowers a child's flourishing.

The editors' introduction argues that the unifying theme of Lee's films is the struggle for authentic self-identity, framed through Charles Taylor's dialogical self and Kierkegaard's line that anxiety is the dizziness of freedom. It surveys how Confucian virtues (ren, li, xiao) and Daoist wu-wei play out across Pushing Hands, The Wedding Banquet, Eat Drink Man Woman, Crouching Tiger, Sense and Sensibility, Brokeback Mountain and others, treating each protagonist as caught between traditional obligation and personal desire. It invokes Nietzsche's claim that all philosophy is autobiography to justify reading Lee's films (he said 'it's all in my films') as a coherent authorial philosophy.

McRae reads Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon as a dramatization of the tension between Confucian humanism and Daoist naturalism over how to cultivate an authentic 'focus-field' self. Li Mu Bai and Yu Shu Lien are exemplary persons (junzi) bound by the wuxia code and li, unable to voice their love, while Jen rebels into criminal freedom under Jade Fox; Li's use of the green bamboo forest against Jen embodies wu-wei and rou (yielding suppleness). It argues that authentic self-cultivation, and Jen's final leap, require balancing Daoist natural freedom against Confucian roles, since freedom without relationships exacts a fatal price.

Kohler-Ryan and Palmer treat 'sense' and 'sensibility' as a spectrum Lee explores through sisterhood in Sense and Sensibility (Elinor/Marianne) and Crouching Tiger (Shu Lien/Jen). Elinor and Shu Lien embody sense, Shu Lien specifically the Confucian balance of li and ren that lets her soften ritual with humanity; Marianne embodies Burke's British-Romantic sublime while Jen embodies Daoist immersion in the dao. Reading door-frames, windows, hair-combing rituals and Shu Lien's hairpin as symbols, they argue only Sense and Sensibility achieves integration in time, whereas Li Mu Bai's confession that he lived sense and sensibility as separate spheres comes too late.

Thompson argues that Lee's 'cowboy aesthetic' of rugged isolation in Brokeback Mountain (Ennis and Jack) and Crouching Tiger (Li Mu Bai, Shu Lien, Jen) is only apparent: the characters are always already embedded in Confucius' five cardinal relationships, read through Xunzi's darker view that selfish desire must be curbed by ritual and social hierarchy. Ennis and Jack seem lone individuals but are defined by ties to Alma, family and each other, and Jen's redemption comes when she abandons self-serving desire to re-establish her Confucian relationships. Citing Nietzsche's gloss on Aristotle that only a beast or a god lives alone, it concludes there is no truly isolated cowboy.

Bush argues that Brokeback Mountain transcends both the heterosexual western archetype and queer theory by presenting male sexuality through Mencius' philosophy and John Corvino's ethics of homosexuality. Using Mencius' four sprouts (ren, li, yi, zhi) and doctrine of natural goodness, he reads Ennis as the character in whom sexuality is contextual, cultivated and moral rather than merely physical, so the relationship between Ennis and Jack becomes an ethical friendship grounded in ren, the virtue Mencius says is most intense among friends. The bystanders Aguirre and Alma keeping the secret, and the final shirt-and-postcard scene, illustrate zhi as contextual moral judgment and homosexuality reframed as ethical rather than sexual.

Jameson and Brace read Sense and Sensibility and Brokeback Mountain through Burke's and Gilpin's aesthetics of the sublime, the beautiful and the picturesque, mapped onto the Chinese yin/yang and qi of landscape. In Sense and Sensibility, manicured French/Brownian gardens (beautiful, sanctioned) versus wild picturesque nature (sublime, passionate) mirror Elinor's controlled sense and Marianne's storm-caught sensibility, with Willoughby's rescue and Brandon's steadiness keyed to landscape. In Brokeback Mountain the masculine sublime wilderness (yang) versus feminine confining civilization (yin) is built through tightly framed interiors, sweeping exteriors and an 'aesthetics of isolation' that exposes American freedom as a costly illusion for Ennis and Jack.

samples: Elkholy's editorial introduction defines 'Beat' (the New York/West Coast writers) versus 'beat' (a lifestyle of weariness and disaffiliation), tracing the term through Kerouac, Ginsberg's 'Howl,' and Snyder. She frames the Beats' turning-inward and self-marginalization philosophically, noting that Brustein's charge that beats pursue aimless 'kicks' echoes Kierkegaard's critique of the Romantics as engaged in purposeless, rootless striving that evades responsibility. Against this she sets Holmes's reading of beat detachment as a search for meaning and belief, and casts the Beats' global travels as anticipating an emerging cosmopolitanism.

Scribner uses Ginsberg's 'Howl for Carl Solomon'—and Solomon's throwing potato salad at a Dada lecture—to ask whether the Beats' performative acts count as philosophy at all. He argues philosophy is constituted by self-contestation, its relation to a 'non-philosophy' of madness and raw experience, reading Solomon's silence and Ginsberg's poetic mediation through Foucault's 'Madness and Civilization' and Derrida's rebuttal in 'Cogito and the History of Madness.' Ginsberg-to-Solomon is made analogous to philosophy-to-the-Beats: a betraying translator who nonetheless must give the mute event voice, grounded in Plato's failure to banish the poets from the Republic.

Quinn reads Diane di Prima's serial poem 'Loba' and 'Memoirs of a Beatnik' through Hélène Cixous's 'The Laugh of the Medusa' and its call to 'écriture féminine'—women writing the body. She argues di Prima's she-wolf/Medusa figure, sex-positive candor, and refusal of narrative closure enact Cixous's boundless feminine writing, while Cixous's anti-Freudian, anti-Lacanian mockery of 'penis envy' and the 'big dick' illuminates di Prima's transgressive motherhood and bisexuality. Against the male Beats' dismissal of women writers (and Beauvoir's foremother status), the essay centralizes di Prima as a serious feminist philosopher-poet rather than a nostalgic icon.

Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.

Hayes reads Gary Snyder's poetry and prose on 'being-at-home' through Heidegger's claim that 'poetically man dwells' and his earth/world distinction, arguing Snyder's bioregionalism (renaming California the 'Shasta Bioregion,' America 'Turtle Island') roots identity in place while embracing Zen impermanence learned from Dōgen. Snyder's shamanic 'tawny grammar,' his pragmatic environmental program in 'Four Changes,' and his Transcendentalist lineage (Thoreau, Emerson) turn wildness into 'the state of complete awareness,' letting a place 'set free into its own presencing' and grounding a poetics of dwelling that is at once local, geological, and impermanent.

Bolton argues William S. Burroughs's fragmented subjects—split by a parasitic 'Other Half' or word virus—are not postmodernism's dissolved nonsubjects but practitioners of a productive self-alienation. He aligns Burroughs's multiply-named, body-swapping characters (Mr. Bradley Mr. Martin, Joe the Dead) with Lacan's split subject constituted in language and with Derrida's iterable 'mark' and 'third that walks beside you' as an absent-present that dissolves binaries. Through Naked Lunch, Nova Express, and The Western Lands the Burroughsian subject transmigrates from Marxian/Hegelian alienation to N. Katherine Hayles's posthuman, gaining agency by extending into its technologized environment.

samples: LaRocca frames the whole volume around Kaufman's recurring 'who-what-why' of selfhood, arguing that his films literalize an inner alterity in which we are others to ourselves. He runs through Being John Malkovich (a homunculus inside another's head), Adaptation (a genetic twin), and Eternal Sunshine (memory as the very definition of who one is) to show doubling as Kaufman's method, and lists eternal recurrence among the philosophical conundra Kaufman embeds in flawed characters. The essay reads Kaufman's pseudonymity and self-naming as intensifying, not closing, the gap between the self and its double.

Evans reads Adaptation as a creation story: the character Charlie Kaufman must make a script 'out of nothing' rather than transcribe Susan Orlean's Orchid Thief, so the film enacts Deleuze's idea of the writer as fabulator who confronts the audience with the text as invention. She sets Charlie's Genesis-like 'beginning without end' against Donald and Robert McKee's Aristotelian, plot-driven Story where the ending justifies the means (glossing MacIntyre's 'stories are lived before they are told'). Naming the character after himself, she argues, marks the distance between imaginative making (poesis) and Orlean's realist journalism (mimesis).

Falzon argues that Being John Malkovich stages the Cartesian self as a nonbodily homunculus — Craig 'riding' behind Malkovich's eyes via the vision-limiting cutout and muffled audio — only to expose its absurdity when Malkovich enters his own portal and finds a world reduced to 'Malkovich, Malkovich.' As Craig learns to fully inhabit and puppeteer the body, the film shifts to Merleau-Ponty's and Dewey's embodied 'lived body' organized by habit. Reading Craig's takeover as Foucauldian subjectification through training, Falzon contrasts Craig's self-entrapping mastery with Lotte's genuine self-transcendence, her openness to being other than herself.

Von der Ruhr reads Human Nature through Kafka's 'A Report to an Academy,' whose humanized ape frames the film's inverted arc (Puff raised as ape, civilized by Nathan, then reverted by Lila). Using Nietzsche's herd passage and Norman Malcolm on animal thought, he argues the human–animal difference is one of kind, so Lila's Rousseauian idealization of Puff as 'uncontaminated by civilization' and Puff's claim that 'words are evil' are confused. Invoking Wittgenstein's view that art should teach and that lying presupposes truth-telling, he faults the film's bleak, self-referential loves while crediting it as a mirror of the viewer's own thinking.

LaRocca uses Chuck Barris's claim to be a CIA assassin to argue that autobiography makes truth rather than reports fact: unlike the earnest Confessions of Augustine and Rousseau, Barris flaunts the narrator's unreliability, and (following Stanley Fish) the autobiographer 'cannot lie' because whatever he writes is the truth about himself. Kaufman amplifies Barris's love of Carlyle's Sartor Resartus — 'the tailor, retailored' — to cast writing as patchwork quotation, contrasting Nietzsche's 'drive to truth' against literary truth. The essay closes on Clooney's literalizing adaptation, which deauthorized Kaufman, to reopen the auteur-vs-screenwriter question of who authored the film.

Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
